design_detail: Naturalistic field study of two self-selected groups of people who use ketamine, each tested twice, without a measurement before use and without a group that does not use ketamine: 18 who said they used ketamine more than twice a month (frequent group) and 19 who said twice a month or less (infrequent group), all of whom reported having taken ketamine within 30 minutes before the first testing. Recruited at clubs and squat parties; tested on the night of use (day 0) and retested after 3 days (day 3), usually at home, with the battery of Curran and Morgan (2000) without word-stem completion (prose recall, letter and category fluency, speed of comprehension, serial sevens, digit cancellation; adapted CADSS, state schizotypy questionnaire, mood scale, 12 symptom ratings), plus impulsivity and personality questionnaires on day 3. Participants were people who use drugs recreationally, tested where they were using them; neither laboratory volunteers given a known dose nor patients. Repeated-measures ANOVA, group (between) by day (within), with the day-0 amount and years of use as covariates where groups differed. Classed as a short prospective cohort, as for sc_curran_2000; the exposure contrast is usual frequency of use, so the day-3 comparison is in effect cross-sectional.
can_establish: Whether, among 37 people tested within 30 minutes of self-reported ketamine use at clubs or squat parties, those who said they used ketamine frequently differed from those who used it infrequently on memory, attention, self-rated dissociation, psychosis-like experiences and mood that night and 3 days later.
cannot_establish: That frequent use caused the lower prose recall and category fluency on day 3 (no measurement before use, self-reported and unverified use, and groups that differed in education, employment, alcohol on the test night and amphetamine use); that the differences last beyond 3 days; or that they amount to impairment or to everyday memory problems, since there was no group that does not use ketamine, no comparison with norms and no measure of everyday memory.

sample.recruitment: Community: clubs and squat parties, snowball sampling, with participation confidential (p. 751); the Discussion says the sample came mainly from squat parties (p. 758). City, number of venues and recruitment period not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: People who used several drugs and reported having taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before taking part; frequent use defined as more than twice a month and infrequent use as twice a month or less, a cut-off based on Curran and Morgan (2000) (p. 751). No other inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated; unlike the 2000 study, no one is said to have been excluded for other drugs taken that night or before the retest.
sample.demographics: 28 men and 9 women (5 women in the frequent and 4 in the infrequent group); mean age 24.8 (SD 3.8) and 26.2 (SD 8.7), t(35) = −0.65. Highest qualification, frequent/infrequent: none 2/0, City and Guilds 0/4, GCSE 12/5, A-levels 4/6, degree 0/4. Employment: unemployed 7/4, manual or retail work 9/6, skilled work 2/4, students 0/5 (p. 753).
sample.attrition: Reported only as 37 participants completing the study (p. 751); how many were tested on day 0 and not retested is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers at clubs and squat parties, willing to be tested while intoxicated, grouped by self-reported usual frequency. The frequent group was less educated (no degree holders against 4 of 19; GCSE as the highest qualification in 12 of 18 against 5 of 19), more often unemployed (7 against 4) and included no students (against 5), so frequency of use is entangled with education and social circumstances; the authors acknowledge the education difference (pp. 757–758).

exposure.measurement: Self-report: on day 3 everyone again reported day-0 use, and a drug use questionnaire recorded current use of ketamine and other drugs and drug history (pp. 752–753). No biological or drug-sample testing; the authors take the characteristic profile of subjective effects as strong support that ketamine was actually taken (p. 759).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported by participants, not amounts given by the study (Table 1, p. 754): amount taken on day 0 before testing 0.19 g (SD 0.07) in the frequent and 0.11 g (SD 0.07) in the infrequent group (t(35) = 3.42, p = 0.002); usual amount per session 0.58 g (SD 0.43) and 0.21 g (SD 0.48); days of use per month 13.53 (SD 6.18) and 0.45 (SD 0.80); years of regular use 1.94 (SD 1.26) and 0.89 (SD 1.23). Five people in the frequent group reported use on 20–24 days a month (p. 758). Content of the material unknown; route not recorded; whether more was taken after the day-0 testing is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Test night (day 0): cannabis in 7 frequent and 10 infrequent participants (mean 1.3 and 1.4 joints), alcohol in 10 and 4 (mean 0.7 and 1.2 drinks), amphetamine in 2 frequent and ecstasy in 2 infrequent participants. Day 3: cannabis in 8 and 7, alcohol in 8 and 4 (1–3 units), without a statement of whether this came before the retest (p. 753). Usual use, days per month, frequent and infrequent: cannabis 17.4 and 19.0, alcohol 15.2 and 14.2, MDMA 2.8 and 2.0; amphetamine 20 days a month in two members of the frequent group and otherwise 4.5 and 1.5; LSD 2 and 1.3; cocaine 0.4 and 0.74; very little use of other drugs (pp. 753–754). No tests of these differences are reported and nothing is adjusted.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Day 0 was measured during intoxication. When consenting, participants had promised in writing to take no ketamine before the retest, and all said afterwards that they had taken none; 15 reported cannabis and 12 alcohol on day 3. Nothing was verified (pp. 752–753).

comparison.controls: No group that does not use ketamine: the infrequent group (twice a month or less; mean 0.45 days a month) is the comparison for the frequent group. Both groups had taken ketamine before the day-0 testing and were tested in the same way on the same schedule.
comparison.matching: Not matched or adjusted for education, employment or other drug use. Similar age and sex mix; the authors report no group differences on the impulsivity and personality questionnaires without giving scores (p. 756). Alcohol on the test night 10 of 18 against 4 of 19 (editors' Fisher exact test p = 0.045). The day-0 amount and years of use were entered as covariates where groups differed (p. 753).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before ketamine use and no estimate of premorbid IQ or reading ability, although the groups differed in education; psychiatric history not recorded.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Both groups used several drugs, by self-report roughly similarly for cannabis, alcohol and MDMA, but amphetamine use was three times as frequent in the frequent group even without the two people who used it 20 days a month (4.5 against 1.5 days a month), and alcohol use on the test night differed.

outcomes.instruments: Same order on both days; day 0 in a quiet room at the club or party, during intoxication; day 3 usually in the participant's home (pp. 751–752). Cognitive tests (p. 752): Rivermead prose passage, recalled immediately and after about 15 minutes filled with other tests (episodic memory; one point per complete idea, half points for partial recall; maximum 21); letter fluency (R or M) and category fluency (fruit, vegetables), 90 s each, correct words and errors (semantic memory, frontal function); speed of comprehension test (100 sentences judged for sense in 2 minutes; semantic memory); serial sevens for 90 s (concentration and working memory); digit cancellation, deleting 40 target digits among 400 (focused attention), time and errors. Self-ratings (pp. 752–753): adapted CADSS (the 19 self-rated items of the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale, each rated 1–5 and summed); Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire (30 items, state version, true for you "at this moment", each rated 1–5 and summed); Bond–Lader mood scale (16 visual analogue scales; alertness, contentedness, calmness); Subjective Effects Scale (12 visual analogue scales of symptoms induced by drugs such as ketamine). Day 3 only: Barratt Impulsiveness Scale and an Eysenck personality questionnaire (p. 753).
outcomes.validity_norms: No norms used and no group that does not use ketamine. The state schizotypy questionnaire and the self-rated CADSS adaptation are the unvalidated versions of Curran and Morgan (2000). For the everyday relevance of prose recall the authors cite a validation study (Sunderland et al.) whose title in the reference list concerns elderly adults (p. 760).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' means a lower score in the frequent than in the infrequent group, and 'persisting' or 'long-lasting' a difference on day 3. A chronic effect was to be inferred if, 3 days after use, the frequent group showed more memory impairment and higher dissociative and psychotic-like symptoms than the infrequent group (p. 751).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, and no significance level is stated (the 2000 study used p<0.01). Editors' count: 12 cognitive scores (Table 2), 5 self-rating scores (Table 3), 12 symptom ratings (Table 4) and the two questionnaires given on day 3, each tested for group, day and interaction; correlations computed separately by group, the number not stated. The category-fluency interaction (editors' p ≈ 0.048) and the delayed-recall interaction (editors' p ≈ 0.014) would not pass p<0.01.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Drug history was recorded on day 3, at the retest session; whether the tester knew a participant's frequency group when testing and scoring (prose recall scoring involves judgment) is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: F values (df 1,35) and p values only. Editors' calculation from Table 2 (independent t-tests with pooled SD, n 18 and 19; Hedges' g with approximate 95% CI; negative = frequent group lower). Day 0, during intoxication: immediate recall g −0.10 (−0.75 to 0.54); delayed recall −0.30 (−0.95 to 0.34); category fluency −0.13 (−0.78 to 0.51); letter fluency −1.03 (−1.72 to −0.35); speed of comprehension −0.53 (−1.18 to 0.13). Day 3: immediate recall −1.46 (−2.18 to −0.73), mean difference −4.60 points (−6.66 to −2.54); delayed recall −1.15 (−1.85 to −0.46), −3.66 points (−5.73 to −1.59); category fluency −1.15 (−1.85 to −0.45); letter fluency −1.37 (−2.08 to −0.65); speed of comprehension −0.50 (−1.16 to 0.15); serial sevens −0.16 (−0.81 to 0.49); cancellation time +0.33 (−0.32 to 0.98). Dissociation and schizotypy totals: g between −0.2 and +0.2 on both days. Symptom ratings on day 3, frequent group higher: impaired memory +0.97 (0.29 to 1.65); impaired concentration +0.96 (0.28 to 1.64); depression +0.52 (−0.14 to 1.17).
analysis.covariates: The day-0 amount and years of regular use were entered as covariates for measures with group differences; the authors state that this did not alter the pattern or significance of the group effects, without giving the adjusted statistics (pp. 753–755). Both covariates are aspects of the exposure itself; education, the confounder the authors acknowledge, was not adjusted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (submitted May 2000).
analysis.selective_reporting: The covariate analyses, the impulsivity and personality results and any test of the depression rating are reported without statistics; correlations are reported only where significant, and all of them involve day-0 scores, so whether the amount or duration of use relates to day-3 performance is not shown. The abstract reports the day-3 episodic and semantic differences without the trend-level speed-of-comprehension result or the letter-fluency difference already present on day 0.
analysis.power: Not reported. Editors' calculation: with 18 and 19 per group, 80% power at two-sided alpha 0.05 requires a standardized difference of about 0.95 (about 1.18 at 0.01), so the null results for dissociation, schizotypy, serial sevens and speed of comprehension do not show that the groups were alike.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With both groups intoxicated on the night of testing, prose recall and category fluency were similarly poor and dissociation and schizotypal scores similarly very high. Three days later the infrequent group's recall had about doubled (immediate 9.16 against 4.56; delayed 8.05 against 4.39), while the frequent group's immediate recall was no better than on the night (its delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39), and its category fluency was lower (14.06 against 18.95; interaction p<0.05). Letter fluency was lower in the frequent group on both days by a similar margin; speed of comprehension showed only a trend; serial sevens, cancellation, dissociation and schizotypal scores did not differ between groups, and dissociation and schizotypy were low in both groups on day 3. The frequent group also rated more impaired memory and concentration on day 3. The groups differed in education, employment, alcohol on the test night and amphetamine use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "frequent use of ketamine produces long-lasting impairments in episodic memory" and in aspects of semantic retrieval, and that people using or considering ketamine should be told of these persisting, detrimental effects (p. 749). The Discussion says the results strongly imply that regular use produces detrimental effects on memory lasting beyond the acute effects (p. 756), that people who use ketamine regularly would experience memory problems in daily life (p. 757) and that regular use per se induces memory impairments (p. 758); the closing paragraph says only that frequent use is associated with impairments (p. 759). Gaps: (1) causal and public-health language from a comparison of self-selected groups that differed in education (no degree holders against 4 of 19), employment and other drug use, which the authors acknowledge (pp. 757–758) but do not adjust for; (2) 'long-lasting' from a single retest 3 days after use; (3) 'impairment' and everyday memory problems without a group that does not use ketamine, without norms and without any measure of everyday memory; (4) of the authors' three reasons against baseline differences, the matching is contradicted by the paper's own education and alcohol figures, the claim that the groups performed similarly on speed of comprehension overlooks a trend in the same direction (p = 0.086), and the negative correlations between years of use and memory involve recall measured while intoxicated on day 0, not day-3 recall, and in the infrequent group go with a correlation between years of use and the amount taken that night (p. 756); the third reason is animal evidence; (5) recall near the floor on the night of use in both groups could mask a pre-existing difference that then appears on day 3 as a group × day interaction; (6) the abstract and introduction describe the 2000 study as showing persisting memory impairment and raised psychotogenic symptoms against controls (pp. 749, 751), while that paper attributed its day-3 prose-recall difference to a missed practice benefit.

timeline.event: Curran and Morgan: the same laboratory's earlier field study against polydrug-using peers who had not taken ketamine; it reported day-3 differences on speed of comprehension and category fluency and raised day-3 dissociation and schizotypal scores, and attributed its day-3 prose-recall difference to a missed practice benefit.
This study: frequent against infrequent ketamine use, both groups tested on a night of use and 3 days later.

Three-year longitudinal follow-up by the same group of people who had substantially reduced their ketamine use (per its title; Morgan, Monaghan and Curran, 2004); results to be taken from its own card.
Comparison of frequent, infrequent and former ketamine use with polydrug-using and non-using controls (per its title; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran, 2009); results to be taken from its own card.

One-year longitudinal study of neurocognitive function with chronic ketamine self-administration (per its title; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran, 2010), which has a published erratum; results to be taken from its own card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication of the frequent-against-infrequent day-3 memory difference appears in the sources read for this card (this paper and Curran and Morgan, 2000). Later studies by the same research group that address the question, including longitudinal ones and one with non-using controls, are on this round's list (timeline) and will be appraised on their own cards; their results were not read for this card. Compared with the 2000 study, the acute profile was reproduced, the day-3 rise in dissociation and schizotypy was not, and a day-3 category-fluency difference appeared in both, against different comparison groups.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement. The acknowledgements thank Celia Morgan for helpful comments on an earlier draft (p. 759).
funding.affiliations_note: Psychopharmacology Research Unit, Sub-department of Clinical Health Psychology, University College London (p. 749). The first author led the 2000 study whose interpretations this paper set out to test.

what_would_settle_it: A longitudinal study that measures memory and verbal ability before regular ketamine use begins (or at least estimates premorbid ability), follows people at different frequencies of use verified by hair or urine testing alongside education-matched peers who do not use ketamine, retests everyone after verified ketamine-free intervals of weeks and months rather than 3 days, scores the tests blind and against norms, and includes a measure of everyday memory.

domains.note: Education (no degree holders against 4 of 19; GCSE as the highest qualification in 12 against 5), employment, alcohol on the test night (10 against 4) and amphetamine use differed and none was adjusted; the covariates used (day-0 amount, years of use) are part of the exposure and their adjusted results are not shown. Letter fluency differed by a similar margin on both days, as a stable pre-existing difference would; no baseline before use.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Frequency, amounts and years of use self-reported, without biological verification; content of the material unknown; the frequency cut-off was fixed in advance, but group membership rests on recalled usual frequency.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Snowball recruitment at clubs and squat parties of volunteers willing to be tested while intoxicated.

Cannabis (8 against 7) and alcohol (8 against 4) reported on day 3, timing relative to the retest not stated; further ketamine after the day-0 testing not reported; abstinence from ketamine self-reported only.
Only completers are described; the number tested on day 0 and lost is not reported.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Prose recall and fluency are standard tests, but scoring involves judgment, whether the tester knew the group is not reported, the setting changed with the day, and the self-rating scales are unvalidated, with reported means below their stated minima.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No significance level and no correction across 31 measures; covariate, personality and impulsivity results given without statistics; only significant correlations reported, all with day-0 scores; the headline interactions are at p ≈ 0.014 for delayed recall (printed p<0.01) and p ≈ 0.048 for category fluency.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The study can be cited for the acute profile on a night of self-reported ketamine use in frequent and infrequent groups alike, and for the finding that 3 days later people who said they used ketamine frequently recalled less prose and produced fewer category words than people who used it infrequently, with no difference in dissociation or schizotypal scores. It cannot be cited for the authors' conclusion that frequent use produces long-lasting memory impairment: the comparison is between self-selected groups that differed in education, employment and other drug use, without a baseline, a group that does not use ketamine, norms or verification of use, and with a single follow-up at 3 days. Very high risk of bias for the causal reading.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: thirty-seven people completed the study, 18 who reported using ketamine more than twice a month and 19 who reported twice a month or less, all of whom said they had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing. They were recruited at clubs and squat parties and tested that night (day 0) and once more after 3 days (day 3), usually at home, with the same 25–35-minute battery in the same order; the number tested on day 0 but not retested is not reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants and design, 1st paragraph (p. 751); Procedure (p. 751, continuing on p. 752)

key_findings.finding: Self-reported ketamine use, frequent against infrequent group, means (SD): amount taken on day 0 before testing 0.19 (0.07) against 0.11 (0.07) g, t(35) = 3.42, p = 0.002; years of regular use 1.94 (1.26) against 0.89 (1.23), t = 2.56, p = 0.015; days of use per month 13.53 (6.18) against 0.45 (0.80), t = 8.92; usual amount per session 0.58 (0.43) against 0.21 (0.48) g, t = 2.48, p = 0.018. Five people in the frequent group reported use on 20–24 days a month.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 754); Discussion, paragraph on the reported level of use in the frequent group (p. 758, right column, continuing on p. 759)
key_findings.note: Self-reported amounts of material of unknown content (study conditions, not doses given by the study). Editors' arithmetic: the day-0 amounts were about a third (frequent) and a half (infrequent) of the usual per-session amounts.

key_findings.finding: The groups were similar in age (24.8, SD 3.8, against 26.2, SD 8.7; t(35) = −0.65) and sex (5 and 4 women). Highest qualification, frequent/infrequent: none 2/0, City and Guilds 0/4, GCSE 12/5, A-levels 4/6, degree 0/4. Employment: unemployed 7/4, manual or retail work 9/6, skilled work 2/4, students 0/5.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and reported drug use, 1st paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' Fisher exact tests: degree, 0 of 18 against 4 of 19, p = 0.11; A-level or degree, 4 of 18 against 10 of 19, p = 0.09. Not significant in this small sample, but the authors treat the education difference as a possible explanation (pp. 757–758).

key_findings.finding: Other drugs on the test days: on day 0, cannabis had been used by 7 frequent and 10 infrequent participants (mean 1.3 and 1.4 joints), alcohol by 10 and 4 (mean 0.7 and 1.2 drinks), amphetamine by 2 frequent and ecstasy by 2 infrequent participants; on day 3, 8 and 7 reported cannabis and 8 and 4 alcohol (1–3 units). All reported no ketamine between day 0 and day 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reported drug use on day 0 and day 3 (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' Fisher exact test for alcohol on day 0 (10 of 18 against 4 of 19): p = 0.045. Whether the day-3 cannabis and alcohol use came before the retest is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Usual other drug use, days per month, frequent against infrequent group: cannabis 17.4 and 19.0, alcohol 15.2 and 14.2, MDMA 2.8 and 2.0; amphetamine 20 days a month in two members of the frequent group and, without them, 4.5 and 1.5; LSD 2 and 1.3; cocaine 0.4 and 0.74; very little use of other drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reported general drug use (p. 753, right column, continuing on p. 754)

key_findings.finding: Prose recall, means (SD), frequent against infrequent: day 0 immediate 4.67 (2.59) against 5.00 (3.66) and delayed 3.11 (2.28) against 3.92 (2.88); day 3 immediate 4.56 (1.96) against 9.16 (3.86) and delayed 4.39 (1.57) against 8.05 (4.05). Immediate recall: group × day interaction F(1,35) = 13.5, p<0.001, day F = 12.1, group F = 8.4; delayed recall: interaction F = 6.7 (printed p<0.01), group F = 8.56, day F = 24.1. By the authors' statement, covarying the day-0 amount or years of use did not change these results.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Cognitive assessments (Table 2) › Prose recall (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: F(1,35) = 6.7 corresponds to p ≈ 0.014, not p<0.01. The frequent group's day-3 immediate recall (4.56) was no higher than its immediate recall while intoxicated on day 0 (4.67); its delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39 (Table 2; Figure 1, p. 755).

key_findings.finding: Category fluency: 11.83 (4.32) against 12.58 (6.54) on day 0 and 14.06 (3.83) against 18.95 (4.45) on day 3; group × day interaction F(1,35) = 4.18, p<0.05, group F = 5.01, day F = 17.93. Letter fluency was lower in the frequent group on both days, 10.39 (6.01) against 17.42 (7.22) and 14.00 (5.13) against 22.10 (6.36), with group F = 18.5, day F = 35.0 and no interaction.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 754); Results › Cognitive assessments › Verbal fluency (p. 754, continuing on p. 755) and Category generation (p. 755)

key_findings.finding: Speed of comprehension showed only a trend towards lower scores in the frequent group on both days (p = 0.086; day 3: 50.33 (17.82) against 59.00 (16.08)); serial sevens and digit cancellation did not differ between groups; all of these improved from day 0 to day 3 (for example serial sevens F(1,35) = 14.10, cancellation time F = 18.1).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 754); Results › Cognitive assessments › Speed of comprehension, and Serial sevens and digit cancellation (p. 755, left column)

key_findings.finding: Dissociation (adapted CADSS) and state schizotypy were very high on day 0 and low on day 3 in both groups, with day effects only (F(1,35) = 78.1 and 48.2) and no group differences: dissociation 34.83 (21.60) and 39.26 (25.32) on day 0, 4.56 (6.35) and 3.47 (5.56) on day 3; schizotypy 54.11 (30.22) and 53.58 (28.39), then 25.28 (19.80) and 28.95 (21.37).
key_findings.locator: Results › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology (Table 3) (p. 755, right column); Table 3 (p. 756)

key_findings.finding: Mood and symptom ratings: on the alertness factor the frequent group rated more sedation on both days (group F(1,35) = 4.63, p<0.04; day 3: 34.16 (23.01) against 18.23 (12.97)), and both groups were less calm on day 0 (F = 9.33). Impaired concentration showed a group × day interaction (F = 5.79, p<0.025; day 3: 33.11 (26.84) against 12.74 (12.53)); impaired memory a group effect (F = 5.79, p<0.025; day 3: 35.94 (23.09) against 15.42 (18.00)); nausea a group effect (F = 5.37); the other ratings, except depression, showed only day effects. The depression rating rose from 10.83 to 20.39 in the frequent group and fell from 16.79 to 10.21 in the infrequent group, without a reported test.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mood and subjective effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 755, right column); Table 3 (p. 756); Table 4 (p. 757)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation for the day-3 depression rating: t(35) = 1.61, p ≈ 0.12, g 0.52 (−0.14 to 1.17). The direction of the mood factors is taken from the text (higher alertness-factor scores mean more sedation).

key_findings.finding: Correlations, computed separately in each group: in the infrequent group, the amount taken on day 0 correlated with day-0 category fluency (r = −0.65, p<0.003) and with day-0 immediate (r = −0.52) and delayed (r = −0.57) recall; years of use correlated with day-0 immediate (r = −0.46) and delayed (r = −0.56) recall and with the day-0 amount (r = 0.56). In the frequent group the only significant correlation was between years of use and day-0 immediate recall (r = −0.54, p<0.025). No correlation with day-3 scores is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlations (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: All the reported correlations involve scores measured during intoxication on day 0. With n = 19 and 18 their intervals are wide (editors' calculation, Fisher z: r = −0.54 gives −0.80 to −0.10).

key_findings.finding: There were no significant group differences on the impulsivity questionnaire (named the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale in the Methods and the Behavioural Inhibitions Scale in the Results) or the EPQ, both given on day 3; no scores are reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Other assessments (p. 753); Results › Personality and impulsivity measures (p. 756)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the 2000 study's ketamine group used ketamine on average 3.1 times a month, between this study's infrequent (0.45) and frequent (13.5) groups, yet only the 2000 group had raised dissociation and schizotypy on day 3; they suggest a U-shaped relation with frequency of use, or sample differences (2000: mainly nightclubs, 75% university-educated; here mainly squat parties, 28% university-educated).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph on schizotypal symptomatology and dissociation (right column)
key_findings.note: The 28% cannot be derived from this paper's education figures (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that there was no objective confirmation of which drugs at which doses were taken, and that baseline differences between the groups cannot be ruled out, the infrequent group having somewhat higher educational achievement.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph on other explanations of the memory results (p. 757, right column, continuing on p. 758); limitations paragraph (p. 759, left column)

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that ketamine's short elimination half-life means that the dose taken on the night of testing would have been eliminated within 24 hours, well before the day-3 testing, and use this against residual effects of that dose as an explanation of the day-3 memory differences.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, paragraph on duration of effect and half-life (p. 750, right column); Discussion, paragraph on other explanations of the memory results (p. 757, right column, continuing on p. 758)
key_findings.note: The argument does not consider metabolites, after-effects or withdrawal in people using ketamine on a reported 13.5 days a month, five of them on 20 to 24 days (p. 758). The frequent group's higher self-rated sedation on both days, its higher day-3 ratings of impaired concentration and memory, and its nausea (p. 755; key finding 9) fit after-effects or withdrawal as well as chronic effects.

key_findings.finding: The authors attribute the two groups' similar performance on the night of use, although the frequent group reported taking larger amounts that night, to tolerance built up by the frequent group over its longer period of use.
key_findings.note: An explanation offered by the authors and not tested in the study; relevant to any statement that the two groups were affected alike on the night.

reporting_issues.issue: The delayed-recall group × day interaction, F(1,35) = 6.7, is printed with p<0.01 (p. 754), and the immediate-recall day effect, F(1,35) = 12.1, with p<0.001. By the editors' calculation these F values correspond to p ≈ 0.014 and p ≈ 0.0014.
reporting_issues.consequence: The delayed-recall interaction, one of the two headline episodic-memory results, is significant at 0.05 but not at the 0.01 level used in the companion 2000 study; this paper states no significance level.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says 28% of this sample had university-level education (p. 758), but the education figures give degrees to 0 of 18 frequent and 4 of 19 infrequent participants, with 5 students in the infrequent group (p. 753). By the editors' arithmetic, degree holders are 4 of 37 (11%), degree holders and students together at most 9 of 37 (24%), and no whole number of 37 rounds to 28%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-study comparison of education, which the authors use to explain why their findings differ from the 2000 study, rests on a figure that does not match the paper's own data.

reporting_issues.issue: The adapted CADSS (19 items) and the schizotypy questionnaire (30 items) are described as rated from 1 to 5 and summed (p. 752), which gives minimum totals of 19 and 30, but the day-3 means are 4.56 and 3.47 for dissociation and 25.28 and 28.95 for schizotypy (Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The items must have been scored from 0, or the scoring is misdescribed; absolute values cannot be compared with other studies, though group comparisons are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Instrument names are inconsistent: the dissociation scale is the Adapted Dissociative States Scale (ADSS) in the Methods (p. 752), the Administered Dissociative States Scale in the Results (p. 755) and ADDS in Table 3 (p. 756); the impulsivity measure is the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale in the Methods (p. 753) and the Behavioural Inhibitions Scale in the Results (p. 756); the personality measure is the Eysenck Personality Inventory (Eysenck and Eysenck, 1995) in the Methods but the EPQ in the Results and EPQ (Adult), 1975, in the references (p. 759).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the data, but it is unclear which personality instrument was used, and the matching on personality and impulsivity, which the authors cite against baseline differences, cannot be checked because no scores are given.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the infrequent group's day-0 digit-cancellation errors as 9.06 with an SD of 1.52, an implausibly small spread beside the frequent group's 5.83 (SD 7.06) on the same day, and equal to the infrequent group's day-3 mean (1.52).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typesetting error; this cell should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The same statistic, F(1,35) = 5.79, p<0.025, is printed for two different effects: the group × day interaction for impaired concentration and the group effect for impaired memory.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a copying error; one of the two values may be wrong, and the self-rated memory result should be cited from the Table 4 means rather than from the F value.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and introduction describe Curran and Morgan (2000) as showing persisting memory impairment, on episodic as well as semantic tests, and raised psychotogenic symptoms against controls 3 days after use (pp. 749, 751), while that paper attributed its day-3 prose-recall difference to a missed practice benefit; the reference list also gives the 2000 paper a title that differs from the published one and speaks of evidence for persisting cognitive impairments (p. 759).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers who rely on this paper's account of the earlier study receive a stronger version of it than the earlier paper's own conclusions; the 2000 paper should be cited directly (card sc_curran_2000).

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that prose recall is the best laboratory predictor of everyday memory cites Sunderland et al. as 1985 in the text (p. 757) and 1986 in the references, where the title concerns subjective memory assessment and test performance in elderly adults (p. 760).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that people who use ketamine regularly would have everyday memory problems rests on a validation study in another population and on no everyday-memory measure in this one.

reporting_issues.issue: On day 3, 15 participants reported cannabis and 12 alcohol use (p. 753) without any statement of whether this came before the retest, whereas the 2000 study discarded people who had used drugs on the day of the second session.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some day-3 scores may have been obtained after cannabis or alcohol use, unequally for alcohol (8 against 4), which bears on the day-3 memory comparison.

disagreements.first_pass: Editors' calculation: F(1,35) = 6.7 corresponds to p ≈ 0.014, not p<0.01. The frequent group's day-3 recall was no higher than its recall while intoxicated on day 0.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, corrected: the last sentence holds for immediate recall only; the frequent group's delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39 (Table 2, p. 754; Figure 1, p. 755). The rest of the finding, and F(1,35) = 6.7 giving p = 0.014, reproduce.
disagreements.resolution: Verified in Table 2 (p. 754) and Figure 1 (p. 755), both read on pages rendered at 150 dpi. Note corrected.

disagreements.first_pass: Three days later the infrequent group's recall had about doubled (...), while the frequent group's was no better than on the night, ...
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227 (interpretation gap: agree, severe), one detail to correct: the frequent group's recall was no better than on the night only for immediate recall; delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39.
disagreements.resolution: Factual correction made after checking Table 2 (p. 754); the rating (severe) is unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, missed: the authors argue that ketamine's short elimination half-life rules out residual effects of the night's dose by day 3 (pp. 750, 758), without considering metabolites, after-effects or withdrawal in people using about every other day; the frequent group's higher sedation, day-3 impaired concentration and memory, and nausea (p. 755) fit after-effects or withdrawal as well as chronic effects.
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 750 (Introduction) and p. 758 (Discussion), and the ratings at p. 755 and Tables 3 and 4 (pp. 756–757). Added as key finding 14, with the caveat in its note; whether the interpretation-gap text should take it up is left to the senior author (rating unchanged).

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, missed: the authors attribute the groups' similar day-0 performance, despite larger self-reported day-0 amounts in the frequent group, to tolerance (p. 758).
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 758 (Discussion, right column). Added as key finding 15, marked as the authors' untested explanation.
